analysis.one_liner: Creates a single federal watchdog to police credit cards, mortgages, and other consumer loans.
analysis.headline: House committees approved it twice on party-line votes (39-29 and 33-19), but the bill never reached the House floor; a version of its core idea became law in the 2010 Dodd-Frank overhaul.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have pulled consumer protection duties scattered across six federal regulators into one new independent agency, the Consumer Financial Protection Agency. That agency could ban unfair, deceptive, or abusive lending practices, force clearer disclosure of costs and risks, examine both banks and nonbank lenders like payday and mortgage companies, and enforce rules with penalties paid into a fund for victims. It would be funded by fees on the financial companies it regulates, and it would preserve state attorneys general's power to sue lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers using mortgages, credit cards, student loans, payday loans, credit reports, and debt collection services. The bill specifically directs the agency to protect consumers from abuse, unfairness, deception, and discrimination, to give traditionally underserved communities access to financial services, and to restrict forced arbitration clauses. State attorneys general would gain new tools to sue violators.

how_it_helps.text: Consolidates consumer protection functions currently spread across the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency, the Office of Thrift Supervision, the FDIC, the FTC, and the National Credit Union Administration into one agency whose sole mission is consumer protection.
Authorizes the agency to ban unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices in consumer financial products and to regulate how costs, risks, and benefits are disclosed to consumers.
Lets the agency restrict mandatory pre-dispute arbitration clauses that force consumers to give up their day in court.

Preserves and expands state enforcement: state attorneys general can sue for violations, and the bill narrows the federal preemption that had shielded national banks from stricter state consumer laws.
Funds the agency through fees on the financial companies it regulates, and deposits civil penalties into a fund to compensate victims.
Requires banks to collect and report data on small-business lending to women- and minority-owned businesses, published annually.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, payday and nonbank lenders, debt collectors, and credit-adjacent businesses would pay the agency's fees and absorb new compliance costs, and would lose income from practices the agency bans. Some of those costs would likely be passed on to customers as fees.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself acknowledges a real cost: it requires the agency to weigh the potential reduction of consumers' access to financial products and the costs to regulated firms before issuing any rule, and compliance costs would likely be passed to customers as fees.

The bill explicitly does not authorize the agency to set an interest rate cap on any credit product, so high-cost lending like payday loans could only be policed through fairness and disclosure rules, not through price limits.

It adds a new regulator on top of the existing banking agencies, which smaller institutions argued would mean duplicative exams and paperwork; the bill attempts to limit this by authorizing exemptions based on a firm's size and transaction volume.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — one agency whose mission is protecting borrowers instead of one whose priorities include bank safety and profitability — was substantial, especially after a financial crisis caused in part by abusive mortgage lending. The main honest costs are compliance burden, particularly on smaller banks and credit unions, and the possibility of less credit access for marginal borrowers. The bill's design attempts to soften both by allowing size-based exemptions and requiring cost-benefit analysis. The absence of any interest-rate cap is a significant limitation, but not a reason the bill's consumer mission was weak.

outcome.mechanism: The committees approved it twice in October 2009 and Energy and Commerce formally reported it in December 2009, but House leaders took up a broader financial overhaul bill instead and this standalone bill never came to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 8, 2009 by Rep. Barney Frank and referred to the Financial Services and Energy and Commerce Committees.
On October 22, 2009 the Financial Services Committee ordered it reported on a 39-29 vote, and on October 29, 2009 the Energy and Commerce Committee ordered it reported on a 33-19 vote.
Energy and Commerce formally reported the amended bill on December 9, 2009 (H. Rept. 111-367), but the full House never voted on it and it died when the 111th Congress ended.

A version of the bill's central idea — an independent consumer financial protection agency — was incorporated into the broader Wall Street reform bill that the House passed in December 2009 and that became the Dodd-Frank Act in July 2010, creating the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers came out ahead in the end, because the bill's core idea was enacted as part of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law rather than allowed to die; the banking industry won some of the fights along the way, notably getting the bureau placed inside the Federal Reserve and securing exemptions such as one for auto dealers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, via the later Dodd-Frank law

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.role: Chair, House Financial Services Committee; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the Financial Services Committee markup, which approved it 39-29.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the FTC-related provisions
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill, ordered it reported 33-19 on October 29, 2009, and formally reported it on December 9, 2009.

for.name: Obama administration
for.what_they_did: Proposed the creation of a Consumer Financial Protection Agency in its June 2009 regulatory reform blueprint and pushed congressional Democrats to include it in reform legislation.

against.name: House Republicans on the Financial Services and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Voted no in both committee markups, producing the 39-29 and 33-19 votes to report the bill.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and banking trade groups
against.what_they_did: Ran a major campaign against the Consumer Financial Protection Agency, arguing it would overlap existing regulators and restrict credit; Republican committee members echoed these objections.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed the standalone consumer agency as part of the party's blanket resistance to the financial overhaul, and no House Republican supported the underlying reforms in floor votes on the broader bill.

sides.party_line_note: Both committee votes to report the bill fell almost entirely on party lines — 39-29 and 33-19, with Democrats supplying the yes votes and Republicans the no votes.

industries.note: The bill would have put them under a new agency with power to ban abusive practices, examine their consumer business, and charge them annual fees to fund it. Their interest in avoiding a dedicated consumer regulator ran directly against borrowers' interest in having one.

industries.industry: Payday lenders, mortgage brokers, and other nonbank consumer finance firms
industries.note: The bill's definitions sweep in debt collection, money transmitting, credit counseling, and other nonbank financial activity, bringing firms that had largely escaped federal consumer oversight under the new agency's examination and enforcement power. This was the biggest gap the bill closed for consumers.

industries.industry: Credit reporting and debt collection companies
industries.note: Both activities fall squarely within the bill's definition of financial activity, subjecting them to the new agency's rules, exams, and penalties, and consumers would gain a central complaint database covering them.
